title: What is Shenandoah GC (Brooks forwarding pointers, concurrent compaction), and what did Generational Shenandoah (Java 25, JEP 521) add?
shortTitle: What Shenandoah GC is — Brooks forwarding pointers, concurrent compaction — and what Generational Shenandoah (Java 25, JEP 521) added

s1_definition.profdef: Shenandoah is a low-pause-time, mostly-concurrent garbage collector developed by Red Hat that performs concurrent compaction, meaning it relocates live objects while the application keeps running. Historically it used a Brooks forwarding pointer — an extra pointer word per object that points either to the object itself or to its new copy — so that reads and writes always reach the current version during relocation. Generational Shenandoah, delivered in Java 25 via JEP 521, adds separate young and old generations so most collection work targets short-lived objects, improving efficiency and reducing required headroom.
s1_definition.analogy: Shenandoah is a renovation crew that moves desks while customers keep working, just like ZGC but using a different trick. Every file folder has a little "current address" slip stapled to the front (the Brooks forwarding pointer). When the crew copies a folder to a new desk, they update that slip. Anyone picking up the folder follows the slip to the real current copy, so nobody ever reads a stale folder. Generational Shenandoah adds the idea that most folders are thrown away quickly, so the crew focuses on the fresh pile and rarely disturbs the long-term archive.
s1_definition.oneliner: Shenandoah compacts the heap concurrently using a per-object forwarding pointer so references always reach the current copy, and Java 25's JEP 521 made it generational.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Shenandoah is a low-pause-time, mostly-concurrent garbage collector developed by Red Hat that performs concurrent compaction, meaning it relocates live objects while the application keeps running. Historically it used a Brooks forwarding pointer — an extra pointer word per object that points either to the object itself or to its new copy — so that reads and writes always reach the current version during relocation. Generational Shenandoah, delivered in Java 25 via JEP 521, adds separate young and old generations so most collection work targets short-lived objects, improving efficiency and reducing required headroom.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Shenandoah is a renovation crew that moves desks while customers keep working, just like ZGC but using a different trick. Every file folder has a little "current address" slip stapled to the front (the Brooks forwarding pointer). When the crew copies a folder to a new desk, they update that slip. Anyone picking up the folder follows the slip to the real current copy, so nobody ever reads a stale folder. Generational Shenandoah adds the idea that most folders are thrown away quickly, so the crew focuses on the fresh pile and rarely disturbs the long-term archive.

**One line to remember:** Shenandoah compacts the heap concurrently using a per-object forwarding pointer so references always reach the current copy, and Java 25's JEP 521 made it generational.

sections.s2_technical:
Shenandoah, like ZGC, aims for pause times that do not grow with heap size by doing marking and compaction concurrently with the application. The defining historical mechanism is the Brooks forwarding pointer: every object carries one extra reference-sized word at a fixed offset. Normally that word points back to the object itself. When Shenandoah relocates the object during concurrent compaction, it first copies the object, then sets the original's forwarding word to point to the new copy. Any access goes through the forwarding word, so it always lands on the current version even mid-relocation.

To make this correct, Shenandoah uses barriers. A read barrier follows the forwarding pointer to reach the current copy, and write barriers ensure that writes go to the right copy and that the collector sees updates. Later Shenandoah versions reduced barrier cost and, in recent JDKs, moved away from the always-present extra word toward load-reference barriers, but the conceptual model of a forwarding indirection to support concurrent relocation remains the thing to understand.

Concurrent compaction is the payoff. Because Shenandoah evacuates live objects out of the regions it wants to free while the application runs, it reclaims and defragments without a long stop-the-world compaction. The remaining stop-the-world pauses are short init-mark and final-mark handshakes, so pause time stays low and roughly independent of heap size, similar in spirit to ZGC though implemented differently. Shenandoah tends to trade a little throughput and some memory for these low pauses.

The big recent change is Generational Shenandoah, JEP 521, delivered in Java 25. The original Shenandoah was single-generation: every cycle considered the whole heap. Generational mode splits the heap into young and old generations and exploits the weak generational hypothesis, collecting the young generation frequently and cheaply so most garbage is reclaimed without touching the long-lived old generation every cycle. This improves CPU efficiency, lowers the sustainable allocation rate at which the collector falls behind, and reduces the heap headroom Shenandoah needs — the same evolution ZGC went through. You enable Shenandoah with `-XX:+UseShenandoahGC`, and on Java 25 you select the generational mode with `-XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational`.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a card-authorization service that must answer each swipe within tens of milliseconds and cannot tolerate long GC pauses, but it also runs on an OpenJDK build where Shenandoah is the preferred low-pause collector. This is exactly what Shenandoah's concurrent compaction solves — it compacts without a long stop-the-world pause.

Problem 2 — Each authorization creates short-lived request objects that die immediately, while a card-BIN lookup table lives for the whole process. Collecting the whole heap every cycle wastes effort on the stable table. This is exactly what Generational Shenandoah solves — focus on the young authorization churn, leave the BIN table alone.

Our mini-project is a runnable authorization simulator that churns short-lived authorization objects against a long-lived BIN table, logs GC counts and pause time, and prints the Shenandoah flags including the Java 25 generational mode. Classes are `CardAuthSimulator` (driver), `BinLookupTable` (long-lived), `AuthRequest` (short-lived), and `PauseObserver` (reads GC beans and logs collection time).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
shenandoah-auth-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/shenandoah/
            ├── CardAuthSimulator.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── PauseObserver.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags):

```bash
# shenandoah-flags.conf
# Classic single-generation Shenandoah
-XX:+UseShenandoahGC -Xms3g -Xmx3g
# Java 25 generational mode (JEP 521)
-XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational -Xms3g -Xmx3g
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Classic Shenandoah
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -Xms3g -Xmx3g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/shenandoah-auth-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.shenandoah.CardAuthSimulator

# Java 25: generational Shenandoah (JEP 521)
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational -Xms3g -Xmx3g \
     -cp target/shenandoah-auth-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.jvm.shenandoah.CardAuthSimulator

# Confirm pauses stayed tiny
grep -i "Pause" gc.log | tail
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a long-lived `BinLookupTable` of one hundred thousand entries and eight million short-lived `AuthRequest` objects, each consulting the table.

Step 1. The BIN table is built once and, after a couple of young collections, settles into the old generation. If Shenandoah later relocates it during concurrent compaction, its forwarding pointer is updated so every reference still reaches the current copy.

Step 2. The loop creates one `AuthRequest` per swipe with a sixty-four-byte payload. These are young objects that die right after `authorize()` returns.

Step 3. When `authorize()` reads the `binTable` reference and the table happens to be mid-relocation, Shenandoah's read barrier follows the forwarding pointer to the live copy, so the authorization reads correct risk data without waiting for compaction to finish.

Step 4. The young generation fills. Shenandoah runs a concurrent cycle: it marks, then evacuates live young objects to fresh regions while the loop keeps authorizing. The stop-the-world portion is only short init-mark and final-mark handshakes.

Step 5. In generational mode the old-generation BIN table is collected far less often, so the collector spends its effort on the cheap, high-garbage young generation, reclaiming the authorization churn quickly and keeping ahead of the allocation rate.

Step 6. `PauseObserver` logs the collection count and total pause milliseconds. Even after eight million authorizations the total pause time stays low and per-pause time stays short, which the gc.log confirms.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Allocation: 100k-entry BIN table (long-lived) + 8,000,000 AuthRequest (short-lived)
    │
    ▼
  Young generation (AuthRequest churn)
    │ fills
    ▼
  Concurrent Shenandoah cycle
    │ init-mark (STW short) → concurrent mark
    │ concurrent evacuation (copy live objects to new regions)
    │ final-mark (STW short)
    ▼
  app reads binTable reference during relocation
    │ Brooks forwarding pointer / load-ref barrier
    ├─ not moved ─→ read self
    └─ moved     ─→ follow forwarding word → current copy
    ▼
  Old generation (BIN table) — collected rarely (generational)
    ▼
  Low, heap-size-independent pauses
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Shenandoah is Red Hat's low-pause, mostly-concurrent collector, and its signature capability is concurrent compaction — it relocates live objects and defragments the heap while the application keeps running, so it avoids the long stop-the-world compaction that older collectors suffer. The classic mechanism that makes this safe is the Brooks forwarding pointer: every object carries one extra reference-sized word that normally points to itself, but when Shenandoah copies the object during evacuation it sets that word to point at the new copy. Accesses go through a barrier that follows the forwarding pointer, so a reference always reaches the current version even in the middle of relocation. Later versions reduced the barrier cost and moved toward load-reference barriers, but the idea of a forwarding indirection to support concurrent relocation is the thing to understand.

Because evacuation happens concurrently, the only stop-the-world work left is short init-mark and final-mark handshakes, so pause time stays low and roughly independent of heap size, which is the same goal as ZGC reached by a different route. The trade is a little throughput and some memory headroom for those low pauses.

The important recent change is Generational Shenandoah, delivered as JEP 521 in Java 25. The original Shenandoah was single-generation and considered the whole heap every cycle; the generational mode splits the heap into young and old and exploits the fact that most objects die young, collecting the young generation frequently and cheaply so it rarely has to touch the long-lived old generation. That improves CPU efficiency, raises the allocation rate the collector can sustain before falling behind, and reduces required headroom. At National Bank of India I used Shenandoah for a card-authorization service that had to answer each swipe in tens of milliseconds; the concurrent compaction kept pauses tiny while a long-lived BIN lookup table sat untouched in the old generation and the heavy churn of short-lived authorization objects was mopped up by the frequent young collections, which I confirmed by watching the pause ninety-ninth percentile and the degenerated and full GC counts stay essentially at zero.
